cards.front: What is declarative memory, and what two kinds does it come in?
cards.back: Memory you can bring to conscious recollection and state. Its two kinds are episodic (events in a time and place) and semantic (general knowledge).
cards.quote: Declarative memory is memory you can bring to conscious recollection and state.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: {{c1::Episodic}} memory is memory for events placed in a time and a place, such as what happened at breakfast.
cards.back: Contrast semantic memory: general knowledge of the world.
cards.quote: Episodic memory is memory for events placed in a time and a place: what happened at breakfast.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: How is nondeclarative memory expressed, and what does it include?
cards.back: In performance rather than recollection. It includes skills and habits, priming, and simple classical conditioning.
cards.quote: Nondeclarative memory is expressed in performance rather than recollection.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: {{c1::Working memory}} is the temporary, active holding and manipulating of a few items, such as a phone number you repeat while you dial it.
cards.quote: Working memory is the temporary, active holding and manipulating of a few items, such as a phone number you repeat while you dial it.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: What is priming, and which memory class does it belong to?
cards.back: Being faster or more accurate with something you met recently, such as reading a word you saw a minute earlier. It is nondeclarative.
cards.quote: priming (being faster or more accurate with something you met recently, such as reading a word you saw a minute earlier)
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: H.M. traced a star seen only in a mirror. Across three days he improved normally, yet did not remember having done the task. What does this show?
cards.back: The practice left a record shown only in performance, not in recall. His operation impaired forming memories he could bring to mind but spared improving with practice: memory has at least two forms.
cards.quote: Across three days of practice H.M. improved, as people normally do, yet he did not remember having done the task before.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: H.M. is read a short list of digits and asked to repeat it at once. Then his attention is moved elsewhere and he is asked again a few minutes later. Predict both results.
cards.back: Immediate repetition is normal; the delayed request fails.
cards.why: His digit span and working memory were normal, but once attention moved on, almost nothing held in working memory became a lasting declarative memory.
cards.quote: Working memory worked, but almost nothing held in it became a lasting declarative memory.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: A person keeps a door code in mind by repeating it until she types it, and an hour later cannot recall it. Which memory held the code, and why was it lost?
cards.back: Working memory. It temporarily and actively holds a few items; repeating the code keeps it available, but once rehearsal stops or attention moves on it is soon cleared, so it was not there to recall an hour later.
cards.quote: working memory is a small notepad that is soon cleared once you stop rehearsing it or your attention moves on.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: A child tells you she went to the zoo last Saturday, and also that a spider has eight legs. Classify each memory.
cards.back: The zoo trip is episodic (an event in a time and place). The spider fact is semantic (general knowledge). Both are declarative.
cards.quote: Semantic memory is general knowledge of the world: that a spider has eight legs.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: After repeated pairings, a tone alone comes to raise a volunteer's heart rate. Is this declarative or nondeclarative memory, and why is it not excluded for lacking movement?
cards.back: Nondeclarative: a conditioned autonomic response, expressed in performance. Nondeclarative does not mean motor.
cards.quote: Nondeclarative does not mean motor: it includes learning to predict outcomes, such as the weather from cards, and conditioned autonomic responses
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: What is the medial temporal lobe, and which structures does it hold?
cards.back: The inner part of each temporal lobe. It holds the hippocampus, the amygdala, and the surrounding entorhinal, perirhinal and parahippocampal cortex.
cards.quote: the medial temporal lobe, the inner (medial) part of each temporal lobe, which holds the hippocampus, the amygdala and the surrounding entorhinal, perirhinal and parahippocampal cortex.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: H.M.'s main loss was {{c1::anterograde}} amnesia: he could almost never form lasting new declarative memories.
cards.back: He also lost some memories from before the operation, a retrograde amnesia.
cards.quote: H.M.'s main loss was anterograde amnesia: he could almost never form lasting new declarative memories.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: Is "H.M. could learn nothing new" correct? What did he keep?
cards.back: No. He kept language, perception and formal intelligence, learned new skills, and over many years slowly acquired a few new facts.
cards.quote: His language and perception were retained, and formal intelligence testing did not show a general decline.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: What does H.M.'s anterograde amnesia show about the medial temporal lobe, and what does it not show?
cards.back: Some part of it is needed to form new declarative memories. It does not show where memories are stored.
cards.quote: Neither result shows where memories are stored, and how the dependence changes with time is the subject of consolidation.
cards.section: One patient, two ways of remembering

cards.front: Why is a single dissociation, such as H.M. failing recall but passing mirror drawing, weak evidence for separate memory systems?
cards.back: The failed task may simply be harder, and any brain damage may hurt hard tasks first.
cards.quote: Perhaps the declarative tests were simply harder, and any brain damage hurts hard tasks first.
cards.section: Why one patient is not enough

cards.front: Define a double dissociation.
cards.back: Damage to one structure impairs task A but spares task B, and damage elsewhere does the reverse: a crossing of failures.
cards.quote: If damage to one structure impairs task A but spares task B, and damage elsewhere does the reverse, that crossing is a double dissociation.
cards.section: Why one patient is not enough

cards.front: What does a lesion double dissociation show about the two structures, and what does it not show?
cards.back: Each structure is needed for its task in that preparation (species, lesion, task); this does not show the memory is stored there. A crossing of group means supports at least partly separable processes without proving them; only for single patients with noise-free scores is the one-capacity account excluded.
cards.quote: It shows each structure is needed for its task in that preparation (that species, lesion and task), not that the memory is stored there.
cards.section: Why one patient is not enough

cards.front: Why can damage that only turns down one shared capacity, by different amounts, not produce a crossing in single patients?
cards.back: If every task rises with that capacity, a patient below another on one task has less capacity, so cannot score above them on any other task. The order stays fixed.
cards.quote: The order of the patients stays the same on every task, however hard each task is (ties are possible near floor or ceiling).
cards.section: Why one patient is not enough

cards.front: Under a single-capacity account, group X has patients with capacities 0.2 and 1.0; group Y has 0.7 and 0.7. Task 1 is scored as the capacity, task 2 as its square. Compute the group means. Do they cross?
cards.back: Task 1: X = (0.2 + 1.0)/2 = 0.6, Y = 0.7. Task 2: X = (0.04 + 1.0)/2 = 0.52, Y = 0.49. Y leads on task 1, X on task 2: the group means cross with one capacity.
cards.why: Group averages are weaker evidence than single patients, so a crossing of means supports separable processes without proving them.
cards.quote: Group averages are weaker evidence: a group mixing mild and severe cases can cross another group's average with one capacity, if the tasks respond to it differently.
cards.section: Why one patient is not enough

cards.front: In the weather-prediction study (Knowlton and colleagues, 1996), how did amnesic patients and Parkinson's patients do on probabilistic classification and on a questionnaire about the training?
cards.back: Over the first 50 trials, amnesic patients learned the classification like controls but had severely impaired memory for the training. Parkinson's patients (striatal dopamine depleted) showed the reverse: a double dissociation of group means. With longer training, amnesic classification fell behind and Parkinson's patients improved somewhat.
cards.quote: So amnesic patients learned the classification but had severely impaired memory for the training sessions, and the Parkinson's patients showed the reverse.
cards.section: The key experiment: lines that cross

cards.front: Someone argues that, in the weather-prediction study, the questionnaire about training was simply the harder task. Which group's result refutes this, and how?
cards.back: The Parkinson's patients. They failed the classification yet scored high on the questionnaire; if the questionnaire were harder, failing the easier task should mean failing it too.
cards.quote: Then the Parkinson's patients, who failed the easier classification, should have failed the questionnaire too.
cards.section: The key experiment: lines that cross

cards.front: Performance above chance relative to controls: relative score = {{c1::(patient score − chance) / (control score − chance)}}
cards.quote: relative score = (patient score − chance) / (control score − chance)
cards.section: Reading a crossing from numbers

cards.front: Classification is two-choice (chance 50%); a questionnaire is four-choice (chance 25%). Controls score 74% and 81%. An amnesic group scores 71% and 39%. Give each amnesic score above chance as a share of the controls' gain.
cards.back: Classification: (71 − 50)/(74 − 50) = 21/24 ≈ 88%. Questionnaire: (39 − 25)/(81 − 25) = 14/56 = 25%. Near normal on one task, far below on the other.
cards.quote: Step 2: size each loss above chance, as a share of the controls' gain.
cards.section: Reading a crossing from numbers

cards.front: Classification (chance 50%) and a questionnaire (chance 25%): an amnesic group scores 71% and 39%, a Parkinson's group 56% and 79%. Single or double dissociation? Is a chance correction needed to tell?
cards.back: Double. The amnesic group is higher on classification (71 against 56), the Parkinson's group on the questionnaire (79 against 39): the order flips. No correction is needed to see the crossing.
cards.quote: The order flips between tasks, so the lines cross.
cards.section: Reading a crossing from numbers

cards.front: Correcting group scores for chance (with controls above chance) cannot change which group is higher on a task. What does it change?
cards.back: How big each loss looks, and so where a score falls against a fixed cut-off such as half of normal.
cards.why: It subtracts the same chance level from every group and divides by the same positive control gain.
cards.quote: What it changes is how big each loss looks, and so where a score falls against a fixed cut-off, such as half of normal.
cards.section: Reading a crossing from numbers

cards.front: On a four-choice test (chance 25%), patients score 45% and controls 85%. Compare the raw ratio with the score above chance relative to controls.
cards.back: Raw: 45/85 ≈ 53%, which looks like half of normal. Above chance: (45 − 25)/(85 − 25) = 20/60 ≈ 33%, about a third, because a quarter of answers are right by guessing.
cards.quote: Raw scores fool the eye about size, not about whether the lines cross.
cards.section: Reading a crossing from numbers

cards.front: A stimulus is paired with an aversive one. What does a patient with selective bilateral amygdala damage show, and what does a patient with bilateral hippocampal damage show (Bechara and colleagues, 1995)?
cards.back: Amygdala: no conditioned skin-conductance response, but can report the pairing. Hippocampus: a conditioned response, but cannot report the pairing.
cards.why: The crossing is in single patients on one autonomic measure, so it is suggestive, and it does not show the amygdala stores all emotional memory.
cards.quote: Here the crossing is between single patients, on one autonomic measure, so it is suggestive rather than decisive
cards.section: A second crossing, in three patients

cards.front: In well-trained rabbits, what lesion abolished the conditioned eyeblink to a tone (McCormick and colleagues, 1982)?
cards.back: Removing the lateral cerebellum on the same side as the trained eye. The reflex blink to the air puff was spared.
cards.quote: removed the lateral cerebellum ipsilateral to (on the same side as) the trained eye.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: Suppose a cerebellar lesion that abolished a rabbit's conditioned eyeblink had merely paralysed the eyelid. What would happen to the reflex blink to the air puff, and what was actually seen?
cards.back: Paralysis predicts the reflex blink fails too. It was spared, so the eye could still close; only the learned response to the tone was gone.
cards.quote: It would have failed too. It was spared, so the animals could still close the eye; what had gone was the learned response to the tone.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: After a lateral cerebellar lesion abolished a rabbit's conditioned eyeblink on the trained side, the eye on the other side could still be conditioned. Which explanations does this rule out?
cards.back: That the rabbit could no longer hear the tone, and that it had lost the ability to learn at all.
cards.quote: the eye on the other side could still be conditioned after the lesion, so the rabbits could still hear the tone and still learn.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: Why does the rabbit cerebellar eyeblink lesion remain a single dissociation, and what can its controls not rule out?
cards.back: No second lesion showed the reverse effect. The controls cannot rule out that the learned response is simply more fragile than the reflex.
cards.quote: Its controls rule out paralysis, deafness and a general loss of learning, but not that the learned response is simply more fragile than the reflex.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: Rabbits are trained on eyeblink conditioning while a drug silences either the red nucleus (on the output route) or the region around the cerebellar interpositus nucleus. What does each group show once the drug wears off, and what does the contrast show?
cards.back: Red nucleus group: the learned response appears, so they had learned. Interpositus group: no response, so they had not learned. A structure can be needed to express a memory without being where it is learned.
cards.quote: A structure can be needed to express a memory without being where it is learned.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: Lesioning structure Z abolishes a learned response but spares a matched reflex. A colleague concludes the memory is stored in Z. What limits apply, and what experiment would narrow the question?
cards.back: Needed is not stored: a lost response cannot separate a lost store from a cut output route, and a single dissociation leaves fragility open. Silence Z only during training, then test after the drug wears off: if the response appears, Z was needed to express it, not to learn it.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's needed-versus-stored rule and the logic of the 1993 temporary-silencing eyeblink experiment.
cards.quote: because a lost response alone cannot separate a lost store from a cut output route.
cards.section: The eyeblink: a single dissociation with strong controls

cards.front: Why could Scoville and Milner's 1957 surgical series not show that hippocampal damage alone causes amnesia?
cards.back: Every resection that reached the hippocampus also took the amygdala, so hippocampal damage alone was never tested.
cards.quote: But every resection that reached the hippocampus also took the amygdala.
cards.section: H.M.'s own brain: which structure was needed?

cards.front: In a surgical series, memory loss follows only removals that take structures A and B together, and removals of B alone spare memory. Can you conclude that A alone is enough to cause the loss?
cards.back: No. Sparing after B alone argues against B alone, but with A never removed by itself the series cannot show whether A alone is enough or whether B adds to the loss.
cards.why: Same logic as the 1957 hippocampus and amygdala series: an impure lesion may not say which structure was needed.
cards.quote: Removals limited to the uncus and amygdala did not appear to impair memory, which argued against the amygdala alone
cards.section: H.M.'s own brain: which structure was needed?

cards.front: What did the 2014 postmortem study of H.M.'s brain find his resection had removed, and what remained?
cards.back: The anterior hippocampus, most of the amygdala and nearly all the entorhinal cortex were removed. About 2 cm³ of posterior hippocampus remained on each side.
cards.quote: The resection took the anterior hippocampus, most of the amygdala and nearly all the entorhinal cortex.
cards.section: H.M.'s own brain: which structure was needed?

cards.front: H.M. kept about 2 cm³ of posterior hippocampus on each side. Why might it have contributed little, and why is that only a model?
cards.back: Nearly all the entorhinal cortex, the main cortical route into the hippocampus, was removed, so it may have been cut off. Living cell bodies do not show the cells were connected or working.
cards.quote: The entorhinal cortex is the main cortical route into the hippocampus, so the remaining hippocampus may have been largely cut off.
cards.section: H.M.'s own brain: which structure was needed?

cards.front: In the lesion map of memory, which structure is needed for each task: recalling new facts and events, probabilistic classification, eyeblink conditioning, and a conditioned skin-conductance response?
cards.back: Medial temporal lobe; striatum (implicated through Parkinson's patient groups); lateral cerebellum on the trained side (rabbit eyeblink); amygdala (single patients). Each mapping is one task in one preparation.
cards.quote: The lesion evidence supports this map, one task in one preparation per row.
cards.section: Systems that interact

cards.front: In male rats trained on a spatial and a cued-response maze task (Ferbinteanu, 2020), how did training history change which structure supported the tasks?
cards.back: The hippocampus supported both when they were learned close in time; the dorsolateral striatum supported both when learned in the same environment.
cards.quote: Which system does the work depended on the training history.
cards.section: Systems that interact

cards.front: A lab finds that silencing the hippocampus in rats impairs a cued-response maze task usually assigned to the dorsolateral striatum. Does this overturn the memory-systems map?
cards.back: Not necessarily. Which system does the work can depend on training history, such as tasks learned close in time, so the map is a specialization, not sealed boxes.
cards.why: Rests on the 2020 rat maze finding that training history shifted which structure supported each task.
cards.quote: The map is a useful specialization, not a set of sealed boxes.
cards.section: Systems that interact

cards.front: After a cardiac arrest, MRI shows damage limited to field CA1 of both hippocampi. Design an assessment that decides whether the memory deficit is declarative only.
cards.back: Against matched controls, scoring above chance where tasks have chance levels: digit span against delayed recall after 30 minutes; recent against remote memories; mirror drawing over sessions and a priming task. Declarative-only predicts normal span, normal skill and priming learning, poor delayed recall. MRI localization stays provisional without postmortem histology.
cards.quote: A selective declarative deficit predicts normal span and poor delayed recall.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A patient with MRI damage only in CA1 of both hippocampi has normal digit span and skill learning but cannot recall a story after 30 minutes. What can and cannot be concluded?
cards.back: CA1 damage can be enough for a declarative deficit. It does not show CA1 is the declarative memory system, and MRI can miss damage elsewhere, so the conclusion stays provisional without histology.
cards.quote: one patient shows that CA1 damage can be enough for a declarative deficit; it does not show that CA1 is the declarative memory system.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A tone ends, and half a second later an air puff reaches the eye. Will learning a blink to this tone depend on the hippocampus?
cards.back: Yes. A gap between signal and event makes this trace conditioning, which needs the hippocampus and, in people, awareness of the pairing.
cards.quote: In trace conditioning a gap separates them, and that version needs the hippocampus and, in people, awareness of the pairing.
cards.section: When conditioning needs the hippocampus

cards.front: Damaging a single connectionist network with no separate modules produces a double dissociation. What does this imply for reading crossings in patients?
cards.back: A crossing excludes the simple one-capacity account only for single patients with noise-free scores; group averages argue against it more weakly. Neither rules out every single-system account, so a crossing supports separable processes, not separate systems or anatomical boxes.
cards.quote: Plaut (1995) showed that damaging a single connectionist network, with no separate modules, can produce a double dissociation.
cards.section: A crossing without separate boxes
